name: Crimson Spiral

detectability.signature: Layered gravitometric banding with 0.3g differential between strata

proximity: Mild hull vibration as gravity gradients tug unevenly on ship mass
Navigation drift requiring constant course correction
contact: Severe structural stress as laminar layers exert opposing tidal forces
Cargo shifts and unsecured objects become projectiles
Sensor calibration fails as light bends through gravity strata
prolonged_exposure: Cumulative metal fatigue leading to hull micro-fractures
Crew experiences persistent vertigo and spatial disorientation
FTL drive alignment warps beyond safe tolerances

behavior.cycle: Gravity layers shift phase every 47 standard hours

phenomena: Visible red-shifted light refracting through gravity strata, producing the signature crimson banding
Acoustic resonance transmitted through hull contact, described as a deep harmonic drone
Spontaneous crystallization of certain dissolved metals in fuel lines
Shadow duplicates of nearby objects appearing in adjacent gravity layers
hazards: Laminar shear forces can tear apart vessels exceeding 200 meters in length
Navigation becomes unreliable as gravity layers distort inertial reference frames
Emergency FTL jumps within the zone risk catastrophic drive misalignment
opportunities: Gravity strata can be used to refine rare alloys through natural tidal separation
The predictable layering allows experienced pilots to slingshot between strata for fuel-free acceleration
Scientific study of laminar gravity may advance artificial gravity technology
known_incidents: The bulk freighter Kessler's Promise broke apart in 2418 when its 340-meter frame straddled two opposing gravity layers during a phase shift
A research team from the Meridian Institute spent 14 months mapping the strata, producing the most detailed gravitometric atlas of any tidal zone in known space
description: The Crimson Spiral manifests as a vast elliptical region of layered gravitational fields, each stratum separated by razor-thin shear boundaries where opposing tidal forces grind against one another. Starlight passing through the zone refracts unevenly, producing bands of deep red that coil outward in a slow, majestic helix. From a distance, it resembles an enormous wound in space, bleeding light in concentric ribbons.

Ships entering the Spiral encounter gravity that changes direction and intensity every few hundred meters of depth. The laminar layers act like invisible shelves, each pulling in a slightly different direction, creating a disorienting experience where up and down become meaningless abstractions. Every 47 hours, the layers undergo a phase shift, briefly intensifying the shear boundaries before settling into a new configuration that experienced navigators can chart with reasonable accuracy.

The Crimson Spiral has been a known hazard on the Outer Reach trade corridor for over three centuries. Early explorers mistook the red banding for a nebula and paid dearly for their curiosity. Over time, it became both a graveyard for the reckless and a laboratory for the bold. The Meridian Institute's extensive mapping project transformed it from a mere obstacle into one of the most studied gravitational phenomena in the sector.

Today, the Crimson Spiral serves as a proving ground for advanced navigation systems and a source of naturally refined alloys prized by shipwrights across the region. A small flotilla of specialized harvester vessels operates at its periphery, skimming the outer strata for tidally separated metals. Rumors persist of a derelict military vessel lodged deep within the inner layers, its cargo holds allegedly containing pre-war weapons technology preserved by the crushing embrace of the Spiral's heart.
